title: Laughter Born, Rival Sent, Well Secured
summary: God gives Isaac exactly as promised, separates Ishmael from the heir while caring for him in the wilderness, and secures Abraham’s well at Beersheba.
historicalContext: The chapter unfolds in the northern Negeb, the semiarid country between Gerar and Beersheba where Abraham had moved after the ruin of Sodom. Abraham is a hundred years old and Sarah ninety, a full quarter century after the call in Haran. Households of the ancient Near East commonly nursed children for two or three years, and a weaning was a public milestone marking survival past the perils of infancy. Inheritance customs of the period could give the son of a slave wife a claim on the estate unless the father formally released mother and child, which explains the legal edge of Sarah’s demand. Life in the Negeb depended on wells cut into dry ground, so a seized well was a threat to flocks and household alike. Abimelech of Gerar rules a town on the southwestern edge of Canaan, with a military commander at his side, and early non-Canaanite settlers on that coast are already called Philistines.
literaryContext: Genesis 21 resolves the long tension that began with Sarah’s barrenness in 11:30 and reached its sharpest point in the promise of 18:10–14. Three scenes follow one another: the birth of Isaac (1–7), the departure of Hagar and Ishmael (8–21), and the treaty with Abimelech (22–34). The first two are bound by the root “laugh” (tsaḥaq), which names Isaac, voices Sarah’s joy, and then describes Ishmael’s mockery. The third is bound by the root “seven/swear” (shavaʿ), which culminates in the name Beersheba. The chapter mirrors chapter 16, where Hagar first fled into the same southern wilderness, and it anticipates chapter 22: Abraham rises early, a son nears death, the angel calls from heaven, and a parent’s eyes are opened to God’s provision. Abimelech’s return also completes the Gerar episode of chapter 20, turning a story of deception into a covenant of peace.
themes: God keeps His word at the time He appoints
Joyful laughter replacing the laughter of doubt
The child of promise and the child of the flesh
God hears the outcast in the wilderness
Peace with neighbors secured by oath and covenant
Worship of the Everlasting God in a pilgrim land

outline.title: The Promised Son Is Born
outline.summary: The LORD visits Sarah, Isaac is born at the set time, named and circumcised as commanded, and Sarah’s doubt turns to joyful laughter.

outline.title: Mockery at the Weaning Feast
outline.summary: Ishmael mocks at Isaac’s weaning, Sarah demands his removal, and God tells a grieving Abraham that the line will be called in Isaac while Ishmael too will become a nation.

outline.title: God Hears the Lad in the Wilderness
outline.summary: Hagar and Ishmael are sent away, nearly perish of thirst, and are rescued when God hears, opens Hagar’s eyes to a well, and stays with the boy.

outline.title: The Covenant at Beersheba
outline.summary: Abimelech seeks a lasting oath, Abraham raises the seized well, and the two cut a covenant sealed by seven ewe lambs at the Well of the Oath.

outline.title: Calling on the Everlasting God
outline.summary: Abraham plants a tamarisk, worships the LORD as the Everlasting God, and lives as a sojourner in the Philistines’ land many days.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did unto Sarah as he had spoken.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter opens with God, not with Sarah’s body or Abraham’s age. “The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did unto Sarah as he had spoken.” The two clauses say almost the same thing, and the repetition is intentional. A quarter century of promises lies behind them: offspring in 12:2 and 15:4, a son through Sarah in 17:16–19, and a fixed season in 18:10, 14. What God had said He now did. The narrator wants the reader to see the birth first as an act of divine faithfulness and only afterward as a family event.

The verb “visited” describes God turning His attention to someone and intervening decisively. It can bring judgment, but here, as when Joseph later assures his brothers that God will surely visit them (50:24), it brings rescue and blessing. Notice also that Sarah is named twice and Abraham not at all. The woman who had laughed behind the tent door, who had once proposed Hagar as a substitute, is the direct object of God’s grace. Her barrenness, recorded as early as 11:30, is now answered.

This birth ran against the ordinary course of nature, and the New Testament treats it as a work of divine power received by faith. Paul calls Isaac the son “by promise” in contrast to the son “after the flesh” (Galatians 4:23), and Hebrews says Sarah “received strength to conceive seed” because “she judged him faithful who had promised” (Hebrews 11:11). Isaac’s birth is therefore one link in a chain of saving interventions that reaches its climax when God sent His Son. The same Lord who visited Sarah would later visit and redeem His people in the incarnation (Luke 1:68).

The verse sets a pattern for reading the rest of the chapter. Everything that follows, the naming, the circumcision, the separation of Ishmael, the rescue in the desert, and the oath at Beersheba, flows from a God whose word is reliable.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes a superior taking careful notice of someone and acting to change that person’s situation. Depending on context it can mean to muster, appoint, punish, or come to the aid of. When God is the subject and the result is favor, as with Hannah’s later conceptions or Israel’s deliverance from Egypt, the word signals a turning point in which God steps into a life to fulfil His purposes. The Greek Old Testament renders it with episkeptomai, the verb Zacharias uses when he blesses God for visiting His people.

verses.bibleText: For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.” The verse gives the plain facts of conception and birth, then anchors them in two details: age and appointed time. “In his old age” recalls Abraham’s own laughing question, “Shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old?” (17:17). The impossibility was real. Both parents were past the age of childbearing, and Paul speaks of Abraham’s body as “now dead” and of “the deadness of Sarah’s womb” (Romans 4:19).

The phrase “at the set time” connects the birth to the season God had named a year earlier: “At this set time in the next year” (17:21) and “at the time appointed I will return unto thee” (18:14). The earliest promises to Abraham were open-ended: a seed, then a son of his own body, then a son by Sarah. Only at the end did God attach a date. The narrator underlines that the date held. God’s faithfulness includes His timing as well as His intention.

Scripture often presents God’s acts on a fixed timetable: the flood after an announced period, Israel’s departure from Egypt at the end of the 430 years “even the selfsame day” (Exodus 12:41), and the Messiah’s coming “when the fulness of the time was come” (Galatians 4:4). Isaac’s birth belongs to that pattern. A God who controls the calendar of redemption can be trusted when His people cannot see why He delays.

For Abraham and Sarah the long wait had exposed both faith and failure. The birth does not erase that history, but it shows that the outcome never rested on their reliability. It rested on what “God had spoken.”

wordNotes.explanation: The noun מוֹעֵד (moʿed) means an appointed time or appointed meeting. It is the word used when God made the sun and moon to mark seasons (Genesis 1:14), and later for Israel’s appointed feasts and for the “tabernacle of the congregation,” the tent of meeting. In this chapter it echoes God’s exact wording in 18:14 and 17:21, stressing that the birth occurred on a date God Himself had fixed, not merely at some vague future moment.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham called the name of his son that was born unto him, whom Sarah bare to him, Isaac.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham called the name of his son that was born unto him, whom Sarah bare to him, Isaac.” The sentence lingers. It could have said simply that Abraham named the boy Isaac, but it piles up relationships: his son, born to him, whom Sarah bore to him. After years in which Ishmael had been the only son in the tent, the narrator makes the parentage unmistakable. This is the child of Abraham and Sarah together, the heir God had specified.

Abraham did not choose the name. God had announced it before the child was conceived: “thou shalt call his name Isaac” (17:19). Naming the boy was therefore an act of obedience, matching the faithfulness of God recorded in verses 1–2. In Scripture, names given by God often carry a message, and this one preserves the memory of laughter. Abraham had laughed when told of the son (17:17), and Sarah had laughed in disbelief behind the tent door (18:12). Every time the boy’s name was spoken, the household would recall both the doubt and the God who overruled it.

The name also looks forward. In verse 6 Sarah turns its meaning into joy, and in verse 9 its root reappears darkly in Ishmael’s mockery. Isaac’s very name becomes a test of how people respond to God’s gift. Later Scripture continues to treat him as the son through whom the promise would be traced (Romans 9:7), and his birth by divine word anticipates another Son whose name was also given by heaven before His conception (Luke 1:31).

wordNotes.explanation: The name is a verb form from צָחַק (tsaḥaq), “to laugh,” and means “he laughs” or “he will laugh.” The subject is left open; some take it as a shortened prayer that God may smile on the child, while the narrative itself connects it with the laughter of the parents. The same root runs through chapters 17, 18, and 21, first expressing incredulity, then joy, and finally, in the intensive form used of Ishmael, mockery. The name thus gathers the whole story of human response to God’s promise.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac being eight days old, as God had commanded him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac being eight days old, as God had commanded him.” The phrase “as God had commanded him” answers the phrase “as he had spoken” in verse 1. God keeps His word; Abraham keeps God’s word. Grace given is followed by obedience offered. The sequence matters: Isaac’s place in the covenant did not arise from the rite, since he was already the son of promise, yet the rite was the appointed sign that the covenant was his.

Only a year earlier Abraham, Ishmael, and every male of the household had been circumcised on the day God commanded it (17:23–27). Isaac is the first child in the family to receive the sign at the precise age God specified: “he that is eight days old shall be circumcised among you” (17:12). The law given through Moses would later repeat that requirement (Leviticus 12:3), but the practice is already established here, centuries before Sinai. Abraham’s household lived under God’s revealed commands long before they were written on tablets, a point Scripture makes explicitly when it says that Abraham kept God’s charge, commandments, statutes, and laws (26:5).

Circumcision marked Isaac as belonging to God’s covenant people and pointed to a deeper reality. Moses and the prophets called for circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4), and Paul explains that Abraham received the sign as “a seal of the righteousness of the faith” he already had (Romans 4:11). The outward mark was never meant to replace inward trust. Even Jesus, born under the law, was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), identifying fully with the covenant people He came to redeem.

wordNotes.term: בֶּן־שְׁמֹנַת יָמִים (ben-shemonat yamim) — eight days old
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “a son of eight days,” a common Hebrew idiom for age. The precise day recalls God’s instruction in 17:12 and stresses that Abraham followed the command exactly. The eighth day follows a full seven-day week of the infant’s life, and the same timing is later fixed in Israel’s law and observed for John the Baptist and for Jesus.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham was an hundred years old, when his son Isaac was born unto him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham was an hundred years old, when his son Isaac was born unto him.” The narrator pauses to give Abraham’s age, and the number carries weight. Abraham was seventy-five when he left Haran (12:4), so exactly twenty-five years separate the first promise from its fulfilment. He was eighty-six at Ishmael’s birth (16:16), ninety-nine when circumcised (17:24), and now a hundred.

After the flood, human lifespans fell steeply, and fathering a child at a hundred was no longer ordinary. Abraham himself had treated it as unthinkable (17:17). Paul uses exactly this age to describe the strength of his faith: “he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old” (Romans 4:19). The figure is recorded so that no one can attribute Isaac to natural vigor. The child is God’s doing.

The long delay also served a purpose. By the time Isaac came, every human resource had been exhausted and every substitute had been tried. Abraham’s faith had been stretched, corrected, and matured, and the birth stood as unmistakable evidence of what God alone can do.

wordNotes.term: בֶּן־מְאַת שָׁנָה (ben-meʾat shanah) — an hundred years old
wordNotes.explanation: The same idiom as in verse 4, “a son of a hundred years.” Placing the father’s age beside the infant’s eight days sharpens the contrast between the new life and the aged parent. Hebrews describes those born of Abraham as coming from one man “as good as dead,” yet numerous as the stars.

verses.bibleText: And Sarah said, God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Sarah now speaks, and her words are the first recorded joy in her story. “God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me.” The last time we heard her laugh, it was a private, skeptical laugh inside the tent, followed by a frightened denial (18:12–15). That laughter measured the promise by her worn-out body. This laughter measures her body by the promise. The child in her arms has turned incredulity into delight.

The Hebrew is compact and can be read in two ways. Sarah may be saying that God has given her cause for laughter, a gift of joy; and the second line may mean that everyone who hears will laugh “with” her in shared gladness or “over” her in astonishment at an old woman nursing a baby. Both senses fit. The miracle is so improbable that people will smile at it, yet that smile becomes an echo of praise. Sarah does not hide from the amusement; she embraces it because the source of it is God.

Her response belongs with other songs of women whose barrenness God reversed. Hannah rejoiced that the LORD “maketh the barren woman to keep house” (1 Samuel 2:5; Psalm 113:9), and Elizabeth’s neighbors rejoiced with her when the Lord showed great mercy (Luke 1:58). Isaiah later calls on the barren one to “sing” because her children will be many (Isaiah 54:1), and Paul applies that very text to the children of promise in Galatians 4:27. Sarah’s laughter thus becomes the first note of a larger song sung by all who receive life from God by promise.

The change in Sarah shows how grace works on doubt. God did not wait for her to produce a flawless faith before He acted. He kept His word, and His faithfulness taught her to laugh in a new way. Psalm 126 describes the same experience when the LORD restored Zion: “then was our mouth filled with laughter.”

wordNotes.term: צְחֹק עָשָׂה לִי אֱלֹהִים (tsḥoq ʿasah li ʾelohim) — God hath made me to laugh
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “laughter God has made for me.” The noun צְחֹק (tsḥoq) is placed first for emphasis, and God is named as its maker. The laughter is His gift, not merely her reaction. The following phrase יִצְחַק־לִי (yitsḥaq-li) uses the very verb form that sounds like Isaac’s name, so Sarah plays on the boy’s name as she speaks. The preposition can mean “with me” or “at, over me,” leaving room for both shared joy and amused wonder.

verses.bibleText: And she said, Who would have said unto Abraham, that Sarah should have given children suck? for I have born him a son in his old age.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And she said, Who would have said unto Abraham, that Sarah should have given children suck? for I have born him a son in his old age.” Sarah’s second saying has the shape of a small poem. Her rhetorical question expects the answer “no one.” No neighbor, no physician, no sensible person would ever have predicted that a ninety-year-old woman would nurse a baby. Only God said it, and He said it repeatedly.

The plural “children” is striking, since only one son has been born. It may simply be a general expression for nursing an infant, but it may also reflect Sarah’s sense that this one child opens the way to the many descendants God promised. Nursing is mentioned because it is undeniable proof of motherhood. Sarah did not adopt an heir or obtain one through a servant, as she had tried to do with Hagar (16:2). The child was at her own breast.

The closing words, “I have born him a son in his old age,” repeat verse 2 almost exactly, now in Sarah’s own mouth. The woman who had once blamed the LORD for restraining her from bearing (16:2) now testifies to what He has done. Her wonder is the right response to grace, the same astonishment the psalmist expresses: “Who can utter the mighty acts of the LORD?” (Psalm 106:2). Hebrews remembers her, despite her earlier laughter, among those who judged God faithful (Hebrews 11:11).

wordNotes.term: מִי מִלֵּל (mi millel) — who would have said
wordNotes.explanation: The verb מָלַל (malal), “to speak, utter,” is rare and mostly poetic, which lends Sarah’s words a lyrical quality. Framed as a question, it expresses amazement that something so unlikely has happened. Psalm 106:2 uses the same verb in a similar question about the LORD’s mighty acts, showing how this form of speech fits praise.

wordNotes.term: הֵינִיקָה בָנִים (heniqah vanim) — given children suck
wordNotes.explanation: The causative verb means to nurse or suckle. Its mention makes the miracle concrete: Sarah herself feeds the child. The plural “children” may be idiomatic, yet in the setting of the promise it hints at the larger family that would come through this one son.

verses.bibleText: And the child grew, and was weaned: and Abraham made a great feast the same day that Isaac was weaned.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the child grew, and was weaned: and Abraham made a great feast the same day that Isaac was weaned.” Several years pass in a single clause. In the ancient Near East children were usually nursed for two or three years, sometimes longer; a later Jewish mother speaks of nursing her son three years (2 Maccabees 7:27), and Hannah kept Samuel at home until he was weaned before bringing him to Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:22–24). Infant mortality was high, so a child who reached weaning had passed the most dangerous stage of life. The occasion was a natural moment for public celebration.

Abraham marks it with “a great feast,” a banquet with food and drink to which the household and probably neighbors were invited. The feast declares before everyone that Isaac is the son in whom the household’s future rests. The narrative gives no record of any similar celebration for Ishmael, and the contrast would hardly have been lost on the older son, now in his middle teens.

The verse is a hinge. It completes the birth narrative by showing Isaac safely past infancy, and it sets the scene for conflict. Joy and tension sit at the same table. That pattern recurs throughout Scripture: the arrival of God’s promised gift often exposes rivalry and unbelief in those who had a different future in mind. The rejoicing at Isaac’s weaning becomes the setting where hidden attitudes come into the open.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb גָּמַל (gamal) has a broad range: to deal fully with, to repay, to ripen, and, in the passive, to be weaned. The idea is bringing something to completion. A weaned child has completed the nursing stage. Psalm 131:2 uses the image of a weaned child resting on its mother as a picture of quiet trust in God.

wordNotes.term: מִשְׁתֶּה גָדוֹל (mishteh gadol) — a great feast
wordNotes.explanation: מִשְׁתֶּה (mishteh) comes from the verb “to drink” and denotes a banquet. It is used for Lot’s hospitality, Laban’s wedding feast, and royal banquets. The adjective “great” signals the importance Abraham attached to Isaac’s passage into childhood.

verses.bibleText: And Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, which she had born unto Abraham, mocking.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, which she had born unto Abraham, mocking.” The description of Ishmael is long and pointed. He is not named. He is identified through his mother, her nationality, and her former role as Sarah’s substitute in bearing a child to Abraham. The phrasing reflects Sarah’s perspective and reminds the reader of chapter 16, where Hagar, once pregnant, began to despise her mistress (16:4). The old wound has not healed.

The key word is “mocking.” In Hebrew it is a participle from the same root as Isaac’s name, “to laugh,” but in an intensive form. That form can describe innocent play, and the Greek Old Testament translates it “playing,” adding “with Isaac her son.” Elsewhere in Genesis and beyond, however, it most often means laughing at someone or treating something as a joke: Lot seemed to his sons-in-law “as one that mocked” (19:14), Potiphar’s wife accused Joseph of coming “to mock us” (39:14, 17), Israel “rose up to play” before the golden calf (Exodus 32:6), and the Philistines made blind Samson “make sport” (Judges 16:25). The pun is sharp. Sarah had said that all who hear would laugh with her; Ishmael laughs, but not with her. He makes a joke of the child whose name means laughter.

The age gap supports that reading. Ishmael was fourteen when Isaac was born (16:16; 21:5), so at a weaning two or three years later he was about sixteen or seventeen. A youth of that age who scoffs at a toddler being honored as heir is expressing more than sibling irritation. He is ridiculing the claim that this little boy, rather than himself, carries Abraham’s future. Paul draws exactly that conclusion when he writes that “he that was born after the flesh persecuted him that was born after the Spirit” (Galatians 4:29).

The incident therefore has spiritual weight beyond a household quarrel. The laughter of faith and the laughter of contempt stand side by side at the same feast. One receives God’s gift with joy; the other treats it as absurd. Scripture repeatedly shows that the child of promise will meet mockery, and the same is true of those who are born of God’s Spirit in every age.

wordNotes.explanation: A Piel participle of צָחַק (tsaḥaq), the root of Isaac’s name. The simple form means to laugh; the intensive form can mean to play, to jest, or to make sport of someone. Context decides. In Genesis 26:8 it describes Isaac caressing Rebekah, but most occurrences carry a note of ridicule or improper levity. Here the narrative’s outcome, God’s endorsement of Ishmael’s removal, and Paul’s reading in Galatians 4:29 point to scornful laughter aimed at Isaac and the promise he embodied. The participle suggests an ongoing attitude rather than a single remark.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore she said unto Abraham, Cast out this bondwoman and her son: for the son of this bondwoman shall not be heir with my son, even with Isaac.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Wherefore she said unto Abraham, Cast out this bondwoman and her son: for the son of this bondwoman shall not be heir with my son, even with Isaac.” Sarah’s words are blunt and cold. She will not name Hagar or Ishmael. Hagar is “this bondwoman,” Ishmael is “her son” and “the son of this bondwoman,” while Isaac is “my son, even Isaac.” The woman who once gave Hagar to Abraham as a wife (16:3) now refuses her any status above a slave. Her tone shows that the bitterness of chapter 16 has hardened.

Yet the request has a legal and theological core. Customs of the period allowed a father to grant freedom to a slave wife and her children, in which case they relinquished any claim on the estate. Sarah asks Abraham to do exactly that: to release Hagar and Ishmael permanently so that no rival claim could ever arise against Isaac, especially after Abraham’s death. Later Abraham would provide in the same way for the sons of his concubines, giving them gifts and sending them eastward while Isaac kept the inheritance (25:5–6).

The central issue is the word “heir.” God had made clear that the covenant would be established with Isaac, not Ishmael (17:19–21). As long as Ishmael remained in the household as an older son with a rival claim, Abraham’s commitment to the son of promise stayed divided. Sarah’s motives may have been mixed with jealousy, but her conclusion matched God’s purpose, as the next verses confirm.

Paul quotes this verse as Scripture’s verdict: “Cast out the bondwoman and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman” (Galatians 4:30). In his argument the two women represent two covenants, two ways of relating to God. Inheritance by human effort and inheritance by divine promise cannot share the estate. Those who trust Christ are children of the free woman, born by promise, and they must not place themselves back under a system that seeks God’s blessing by the flesh.

wordNotes.explanation: In chapter 16 Hagar is called a שִׁפְחָה (shifḥah), a maidservant belonging to Sarah. Here Sarah uses אָמָה (ʾamah), a female slave who could be a secondary wife within a household. The change of word keeps Hagar’s connection to Abraham in view while stressing her servile status. Paul’s Greek, paidiskē, carries the same contrast with the free woman.

The verb יָרַשׁ (yarash) means to inherit, take possession of, or succeed to property. It is used of Abraham’s anxiety over an heir in 15:3–4 and of Israel taking possession of the land. Sarah’s concern is not only a family position but the covenant inheritance itself.

verses.bibleText: And the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight because of his son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the thing was very grievous in Abraham’s sight because of his son.” The narrator lets us see Abraham’s heart. Sarah’s demand struck him as wrong. The Hebrew says the matter was “very evil in his eyes,” a strong expression of distress and displeasure.

The reason given is simple: “because of his son.” To Sarah, Ishmael was the son of the bondwoman. To Abraham he was his son. For more than thirteen years Ishmael had been the only child in Abraham’s tent, and Abraham had once pleaded, “O that Ishmael might live before thee!” (17:18). He had probably hoped that both sons could be blessed under one roof. Sarah’s demand forced a separation that his affection could not accept.

Scripture does not mock this grief. A father’s love for a son is honored throughout the Bible, as in David’s anguish over Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33). Abraham’s distress also exposes the cost of his earlier decision to take Hagar without seeking God’s counsel. The consequences of that shortcut now fall on people he loves. Yet this pain prepares him for a far harder trial. If parting with Ishmael grieved him so, the command to offer Isaac in the next chapter would test him even more severely. God is teaching Abraham to place every son, and every hope, into divine hands.

wordNotes.explanation: From רָעַע (raʿaʿ), “to be bad, evil.” With “in his eyes” the idiom means that something seemed wrong or distressing to a person. Jonah uses it of his anger at Nineveh’s reprieve. God answers Abraham with the same expression in verse 12, “let it not be grievous in thy sight,” addressing his feelings directly.

verses.bibleText: And God said unto Abraham, Let it not be grievous in thy sight because of the lad, and because of thy bondwoman; in all that Sarah hath said unto thee, hearken unto her voice; for in Isaac shall thy seed be called.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God speaks into the deadlock. “Let it not be grievous in thy sight because of the lad, and because of thy bondwoman; in all that Sarah hath said unto thee, hearken unto her voice; for in Isaac shall thy seed be called.” God acknowledges both people Abraham is anxious for, “the lad” and “thy bondwoman.” He does not dismiss Abraham’s grief, but He tells him not to let it rule his decision.

The instruction “hearken unto her voice” has a history. Adam “hearkened unto the voice of [his] wife” and took the forbidden fruit (3:17), and Abram “hearkened to the voice of Sarai” when she proposed Hagar (16:2). Both times listening to a spouse meant departing from God’s way. Now God Himself tells Abraham to listen to Sarah. The difference is not who speaks but whether the counsel agrees with God’s revealed purpose. Sarah’s harsh words did not express perfect motives, yet her conclusion that Ishmael must not share Isaac’s inheritance was right, and God confirms it.

The reason is the heart of the verse: “in Isaac shall thy seed be called.” The covenant line would be traced through Isaac, not through every physical descendant of Abraham. Paul builds on this in Romans 9:7–8: “neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children: but, In Isaac shall thy seed be called. That is, They which are the children of the flesh, these are not the children of God: but the children of the promise are counted for the seed.” Hebrews quotes the same words when describing the test of chapter 22, because it was this very promise Abraham trusted when he offered Isaac (Hebrews 11:18).

The principle reaches beyond Abraham’s family. God’s people are defined by His calling and promise, not by natural descent alone. The line called in Isaac led to the promised Seed, Christ (Galatians 3:16), and through Him all who believe are counted Abraham’s seed and heirs (Galatians 3:29). Belonging to God’s family rests on grace received by faith, never on birth, achievement, or human arrangement.

God’s command also calls for trust. Abraham must release Ishmael believing that the God who promised Isaac would also keep His word concerning Ishmael. The next verse supplies that assurance.

wordNotes.term: בְּיִצְחָק יִקָּרֵא לְךָ זָרַע (beyitsḥaq yiqqareʾ lekha zaraʿ) — in Isaac shall thy seed be called
wordNotes.explanation: The passive verb יִקָּרֵא (yiqqareʾ), “shall be called” or “named,” means that Abraham’s recognized line of promise will bear Isaac’s identity and be reckoned through him. The verb is related to the naming of Abraham in 17:5 and of Israel in 35:10, stressing that God’s calling determines identity. The word זֶרַע (zeraʿ), “seed,” is collective here, yet as in 3:15 and 22:18 it can narrow to a single descendant, which Paul sees fulfilled in Christ.

wordNotes.term: שְׁמַע בְּקֹלָהּ (shemaʿ beqolah) — hearken unto her voice
wordNotes.explanation: To “hear the voice” of someone in Hebrew often means to heed and obey, not simply to listen. The same idiom is used when Adam and Abram followed their wives against God’s will. Here God makes Sarah’s counsel the course of obedience, since it agrees with His covenant purpose.

verses.bibleText: And also of the son of the bondwoman will I make a nation, because he is thy seed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And also of the son of the bondwoman will I make a nation, because he is thy seed.” Having fixed the line of promise in Isaac, God immediately reassures Abraham about Ishmael. The son of the bondwoman will not inherit the covenant, but he will not be abandoned. God Himself will make him a nation.

The reason given is tender: “because he is thy seed.” Ishmael’s future is secured by his relationship to Abraham. God had already promised that Ishmael would be fruitful, beget twelve princes, and become a great nation (16:10; 17:20). Genesis later records the fulfilment in the twelve sons of Ishmael, listed by name and settlement (25:12–18). The blessing on Abraham spills over even to the son outside the covenant line.

This verse guards against a hard reading of the chapter. Being outside the chosen line of the promised Seed did not place Ishmael outside God’s compassion. God’s election of Isaac was an election to a mission, the bearing of the covenant and the line of the Messiah, not a declaration that Ishmael was beyond God’s care. Later Scripture shows Ishmael at his father’s burial alongside Isaac (25:9), and the prophets envision descendants of Ishmael’s sons, Kedar and Nebaioth, bringing offerings to the LORD’s house (Isaiah 60:7). God’s purpose of blessing all families of the earth includes them.

wordNotes.explanation: גּוֹי (goy) means a people or nation, a community with its own territory and leadership. God promised Abraham that he would become a “great nation” (12:2); here part of that broad blessing extends to Ishmael. Verse 18 repeats the promise to Hagar with the word “great,” and 25:16 describes the result in twelve princes according to their nations.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham rose up early in the morning, and took bread, and a bottle of water, and gave it unto Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, and the child, and sent her away: and she departed, and wandered in the wilderness of Beer-sheba.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham rose up early in the morning.” The phrase signals prompt obedience. Abraham had argued with Sarah’s demand in his heart, but once God spoke, he acted without delay. The same words introduce his journey to Moriah in 22:3, and the parallel is deliberate. In both chapters Abraham rises early to surrender a son into God’s keeping.

He “took bread, and a bottle of water, and gave it unto Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, and the child, and sent her away.” “Bread” stands for food in general, and the “bottle” was a skin container, probably a goatskin holding several gallons. The Hebrew order is compressed, which has led some readers to imagine Abraham setting a small boy on Hagar’s shoulder. The chronology rules that out. Ishmael was sixteen or seventeen, and the sentence is best read as Abraham placing the provisions on Hagar’s shoulder and then giving her the lad, that is, sending the youth with her. Abraham personally loaded the supplies, a detail that hints at his care for both.

“And she departed, and wandered in the wilderness of Beer-sheba.” Beersheba lay in the northern Negeb, where caravan routes ran toward Egypt. Hagar had once fled toward Egypt by the road to Shur (16:7), and she may have intended to return to her homeland now. The verb “wandered” suggests losing the way and straying. Whether because of unfamiliar terrain or exhaustion, she failed to reach the next well before the water ran out. The same word appears when Joseph is found “wandering in the field” (37:15) and in the confession, “I have gone astray like a lost sheep” (Psalm 119:176).

The expulsion is painful to read, and Scripture does not soften it. A slave woman and her son are sent into the desert with what one man could carry. Yet the scene is not abandonment. Abraham acts on God’s promise that Ishmael would become a nation, and the God who made that promise goes with them into the wilderness. What looks like the end of their story becomes the setting of a fresh encounter with Him.

wordNotes.explanation: The intensive form of שָׁלַח (shalaḥ), “to send,” often means to dismiss, release, or let go. It can describe the formal release of a slave or a divorce, and it is the verb Pharaoh uses when he finally lets Israel go. Here it marks Hagar’s legal release from Abraham’s household, matching Sarah’s request that she and her son have no share in the inheritance. Abraham later sends away the sons of the concubines with the same verb.

From תָּעָה (taʿah), “to wander, stray, go astray.” It describes physical straying in trackless country and, in other contexts, moral straying. Here the literal sense is primary: Hagar lost her way in the desert, which explains why the water ran out.

verses.bibleText: And the water was spent in the bottle, and she cast the child under one of the shrubs.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the water was spent in the bottle, and she cast the child under one of the shrubs.” The verse is brief and stark. In the desert, water determines life. When the skin ran dry, Hagar knew what was coming.

The verb “cast” does not mean that she threw her son roughly. The Hebrew word can describe abandoning or setting down, and here it describes a desperate mother leaving her exhausted son in the only shade available. The low bushes of the Negeb gave little shelter, but it was all she had to offer. The Greek translation uses the same verb that Matthew uses when crowds “cast” the sick at Jesus’ feet (Matthew 15:30). Ishmael was too weak to go on, and she placed him where he might die in shade rather than in the open sun.

The narrator calls Ishmael “the child” here, emphasizing the bond between mother and son. To God he is “the lad,” but to Hagar he is still her child. The scene presses the reader to feel her helplessness. She can no longer provide, protect, or rescue. Precisely at that point, where human resources end, God’s intervention will begin.

wordNotes.explanation: The causative of שָׁלַךְ (shalak), “to throw, cast.” Context can soften it to placing, leaving, or abandoning. It is used when Joseph is thrown into the pit and when Jeremiah is let down into the cistern. Here it portrays Hagar leaving her son, expecting him to die, rather than any act of violence.

verses.bibleText: And she went, and sat her down over against him a good way off, as it were a bowshot: for she said, Let me not see the death of the child. And she sat over against him, and lift up her voice, and wept.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And she went, and sat her down over against him a good way off, as it were a bowshot: for she said, Let me not see the death of the child.” Hagar withdraws far enough that she cannot see him clearly, yet near enough to keep watch. A bowshot was perhaps a hundred yards or more. The distance captures the agony of a mother who cannot bear to watch her son die but cannot bear to leave him either. Her words are less a prayer than a cry of despair.

“And she sat over against him, and lift up her voice, and wept.” The repetition of “sat over against him” slows the scene to a halt. Hagar sits and weeps aloud, alone in the wilderness. Her situation is the opposite of Sarah’s at the beginning of the chapter. Sarah laughs over a child given by God; Hagar weeps over a child she believes she is losing. Both women are mothers of Abraham’s sons, and both are seen by the same God.

Scripture often records the cries of the desperate without polishing them. Hagar does not use theological language. She simply weeps. Yet the psalms show that God listens to such cries: “They cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses” (Psalm 107:6). The God who had once seen Hagar by a spring in the same southern desert (16:13) has not forgotten her. Her despair is about to be met by divine attention.

wordNotes.term: כִּמְטַחֲוֵי קֶשֶׁת (kimṭaḥawe qeshet) — as it were a bowshot
wordNotes.explanation: An unusual expression meaning roughly “like the distance of those who shoot a bow.” It sets the distance at the range of an arrow. The image of the bow anticipates verse 20, where Ishmael grows up to become an archer, a quiet sign that the boy will survive.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּשָּׂא אֶת־קֹלָהּ וַתֵּבְךְּ (wattissaʾ ʾet-qolah wattevk) — and lift up her voice, and wept
wordNotes.explanation: “To lift up the voice and weep” is a Hebrew idiom for loud, uncontrolled grief. It is used of Esau after losing his blessing, of Naomi’s daughters-in-law, and of David’s men at Ziklag. The phrase signals that Hagar’s sorrow was public and overwhelming.

verses.bibleText: And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God heard the voice of the lad.” Hagar is the one weeping, but the narrator says God heard the voice of the lad. Ishmael himself had cried out, whether with words of prayer or with the inarticulate groans of thirst. Either way, God heard. The verse turns on that verb. Ishmael’s name means “God hears,” given by the angel years earlier “because the LORD hath heard thy affliction” (16:11). The name now proves true in the boy’s own crisis.

“And the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven.” In chapter 16 the angel met Hagar beside a spring and spoke with her face to face. Here he calls from heaven, the same manner in which the angel of the LORD will call to Abraham on Moriah (22:11, 15). This messenger speaks with divine authority and in the next verse says “I will make him a great nation,” a promise only God can make. As in chapter 16, where Hagar recognized that she had seen “the God that seeth me” (16:13), the angel is closely identified with God Himself. Many readers of the Old Testament have seen in this figure an appearance of the Son of God before His incarnation, the divine Messenger who comes to rescue.

The angel’s question, “What aileth thee, Hagar?” is not a request for information. Like God’s questions to Adam and Cain, it invites the troubled person to face her situation in His presence. It also calls her by name. Earlier in the chapter Hagar was “the bondwoman” to Sarah, but heaven addresses her personally.

Then comes comfort: “fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.” The words “where he is” are tender. God heard Ishmael as he lay under a desert bush, outside the covenant household, apparently cast off. No place is too remote and no person too marginal for God’s attention. The God of Abraham is not a tribal deity confined to the chosen family. He hears the outcast where the outcast is.

That truth reaches its full expression in Christ, who came to seek and to save the lost and who promised that whoever comes to Him will not be cast out (John 6:37). The wilderness of Beersheba becomes a place of grace because God speaks there.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb שָׁמַע (shamaʿ), “to hear,” is the root of Ishmael’s name, יִשְׁמָעֵאל (yishmaʿeʾl), “God hears.” Though the name itself does not appear in the chapter, the narrator twice says that God heard the lad, quietly confirming its meaning. In Scripture God’s hearing is never passive; it leads to action, as when He heard Israel’s groaning in Egypt and remembered His covenant.

wordNotes.term: מַלְאַךְ אֱלֹהִים (malʾak ʾelohim) — the angel of God
wordNotes.explanation: מַלְאָךְ (malʾak) means a messenger. Joined to God’s name it often refers to a heavenly being who speaks as God and in God’s name, as here when he promises to make Ishmael a nation. Jacob later speaks of “the angel of God” who said, “I am the God of Bethel,” showing how closely the messenger and God are identified.

verses.bibleText: Arise, lift up the lad, and hold him in thine hand; for I will make him a great nation.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Arise, lift up the lad, and hold him in thine hand; for I will make him a great nation.” The angel gives Hagar three commands before giving the reason. She is to get up from her place of despair, lift her son from under the bush, and hold him firmly. Her hand, which had let him go, must take hold of him again. The God who hears does not leave her passive; He calls her back into action on the strength of His promise.

The promise itself repeats what God told Abraham in verse 13 and what the angel told Hagar in 16:10: Ishmael will become a great nation. A dying boy cannot become a nation, so the promise implies that he will live. Faith in God’s word becomes the basis for getting up before the water is in sight. Hagar is asked to trust before she sees.

The pattern is familiar in Scripture. God often tells His people to rise and act before He removes the danger: Israel was told to go forward toward the sea before it parted (Exodus 14:15), and Elijah was told to arise and eat before his long journey (1 Kings 19:7). The command and the promise belong together. God’s word gives strength to do what He commands.

wordNotes.term: הַחֲזִיקִי אֶת־יָדֵךְ בּוֹ (haḥaziqi ʾet-yadek bo) — hold him in thine hand
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “make your hand strong on him.” The verb חָזַק (ḥazaq) means to be strong or to grasp firmly. Hagar is told to take a firm grip on her son, reversing the act of leaving him under the shrub. The same verb is used when God says He holds His servant by the hand.

verses.bibleText: And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water; and she went, and filled the bottle with water, and gave the lad drink.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water.” The miracle is not that water appeared out of nothing. The well was already there. What God created was sight. Hagar, blinded by grief and exhaustion, had sat within reach of the very thing she needed and did not see it. Desert wells were often little more than shafts dug to reach groundwater, their openings covered with stones or brush to protect them from sand and animals. A traveler could pass close to one without knowing it. God showed Hagar what she could not find.

The phrase recalls a pattern in Scripture. When Elisha prayed, God opened the eyes of his servant to see the hills full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:17). After the resurrection, the disciples on the road to Emmaus had their eyes opened to recognize Jesus (Luke 24:31). In each case the reality was present before it was perceived. God’s provision often lies nearer than despair allows us to see.

“And she went, and filled the bottle with water, and gave the lad drink.” The response is immediate and practical. Hagar fills the skin and gives her son water. Life returns where death had seemed certain. The parallel with chapter 22 is clear: there Abraham will lift up his eyes and see a ram caught in a thicket, God’s provision for his son. Both parents of Abraham’s sons see God’s gift at the moment of crisis.

The verse anticipates the gospel’s offer of living water. Jesus told a woman at a well that He could give water springing up into everlasting life (John 4:10, 14), and the Bible’s final invitation calls the thirsty to take “the water of life freely” (Revelation 22:17). The need of every person is not only for the water but for opened eyes to see the One who gives it.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפְקַח אֱלֹהִים אֶת־עֵינֶיהָ (wayyifqaḥ ʾelohim ʾet-ʿeneha) — and God opened her eyes
wordNotes.explanation: The verb פָּקַח (paqaḥ) means to open the eyes, either physically or in the sense of granting perception. It appears in the Eden story, where the serpent promised that eyes would be opened, and in Elisha’s prayer for his servant. Here God grants Hagar the ability to see what was already present.

verses.bibleText: And God was with the lad; and he grew, and dwelt in the wilderness, and became an archer.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God was with the lad; and he grew, and dwelt in the wilderness, and became an archer.” The statement “God was with the lad” is remarkable. The same phrase is used of Joseph in Egypt, of David as a young man, and of the child Samuel (39:2; 1 Samuel 3:19; 18:14). It denotes divine favor, protection, and blessing. Ishmael has been removed from the covenant household, but not from God’s care.

Ishmael grew up in the wilderness and became skilled with the bow. This fits the description given before his birth that he would be “a wild man,” a free-roaming figure whose hand would be against every man (16:12). His life would be that of a desert hunter and warrior rather than a settled herdsman. Isaiah later mentions the archers of Kedar, one of Ishmael’s sons, as famous fighters (Isaiah 21:17).

God’s presence with Ishmael fulfills the promise of verse 13, and it shows the breadth of divine mercy. Election to carry the covenant line did not exhaust God’s goodness. He made the sun rise on Ishmael too and supplied his needs in a hard land.

wordNotes.explanation: The phrase combines a verb that may mean “to shoot” with a noun for a bowman, describing an expert archer. Skill with the bow was essential for hunting and defense in the desert. The same lifestyle marked Esau, another elder son who lived by hunting.

verses.bibleText: And he dwelt in the wilderness of Paran: and his mother took him a wife out of the land of Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he dwelt in the wilderness of Paran: and his mother took him a wife out of the land of Egypt.” Paran was a large desert region in the Sinai peninsula, south of Canaan and west of Edom. Israel would later pass through it after leaving Sinai (Numbers 10:12). Ishmael made his home there, outside the land promised to Abraham’s covenant line, though close to its southern border.

Hagar arranged her son’s marriage, as was customary for parents. She chose an Egyptian wife, drawing on her own people and homeland. The contrast with Isaac is noticeable. Abraham would send his servant back to Mesopotamia to find a wife for Isaac from his own kindred, specifically refusing a Canaanite wife (24:3–4). Ishmael’s Egyptian marriage confirms that his line will develop apart from the covenant family. It is not a condemnation of Ishmael’s worth but a sign that his destiny lies on a different path.

With this verse Ishmael’s story fades from the narrative until he reappears at Abraham’s burial (25:9) and in the list of his descendants (25:12–18). The focus returns to Abraham and Isaac. Yet the account has made clear that God’s mercy followed the son outside the covenant line into the desert, and that His promises to Ishmael were as faithful as those to Isaac.

wordNotes.term: מִדְבַּר פָּארָן (midbar paran) — the wilderness of Paran
wordNotes.explanation: A broad wilderness region south of Canaan, between Edom and the Egyptian frontier. It is mentioned in Israel’s wilderness journey and as the place from which the spies were sent. Moses’ blessing speaks of God shining forth from Mount Paran.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass at that time, that Abimelech and Phichol the chief captain of his host spake unto Abraham, saying, God is with thee in all that thou doest:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass at that time, that Abimelech and Phichol the chief captain of his host spake unto Abraham.” The scene shifts from the desert back to the settled region around Beersheba. “At that time” links the treaty loosely with the events of Isaac’s birth and Ishmael’s departure. Abimelech, the king of Gerar from chapter 20, comes with Phichol, the commander of his army. His arrival with his general gives the meeting a political and military edge. This is a negotiation between powers.

Abimelech opens with a confession: “God is with thee in all that thou doest.” He had seen God’s hand in Abraham’s life firsthand: the warning dream, the closed wombs of his household, the healing through Abraham’s prayer (20:3–18). Since then Abraham had prospered, and the long-promised son had been born. The king recognizes that the God of this sojourner is a power to be respected. The same recognition will be voiced to Isaac a generation later (26:28) and by Laban concerning Jacob (30:27).

The statement shows how God’s blessing on His people becomes visible to others. Abraham did not need to preach to Abimelech to make an impression; the evidence of God’s presence spoke for itself. Proverbs puts the principle simply: “When a man’s ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him” (Proverbs 16:7). Jesus taught that His disciples would be a light whose good works lead others to glorify the Father (Matthew 5:16).

Abimelech’s words also carry irony. The king knew two things about Abraham: that God was with him, and that he had once deceived a king. The request that follows reflects both. Abimelech wants the friendship of a man blessed by God, but he wants it secured by an oath.

wordNotes.term: אֱלֹהִים עִמְּךָ (ʾelohim ʿimmekha) — God is with thee
wordNotes.explanation: The preposition עִם (ʿim), “with,” expresses God’s presence and help. Scripture often uses this formula of those whom God protects and prospers: Isaac, Joseph, Moses, Joshua, and David. In the New Testament its fullest expression is the name Emmanuel, “God with us.” On Abimelech’s lips it is an outsider’s acknowledgment of what God was doing in Abraham’s life.

The name of Abimelech’s commander is not obviously Semitic and may come from Asia Minor or the Aegean world, consistent with the early non-Canaanite settlers called Philistines in the region. A commander by the same name or title appears with Abimelech again in Isaac’s day.

verses.bibleText: Now therefore swear unto me here by God that thou wilt not deal falsely with me, nor with my son, nor with my son's son: but according to the kindness that I have done unto thee, thou shalt do unto me, and to the land wherein thou hast sojourned.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Now therefore swear unto me here by God that thou wilt not deal falsely with me, nor with my son, nor with my son’s son.” Abimelech asks for a binding oath in God’s name. The request covers three generations, a way of saying “permanently.” Ancient treaties often bound the descendants of the parties, and Abimelech wants peace with Abraham’s house not only for his own lifetime but for those who will inherit his throne.

The phrase “deal falsely” is pointed. Abraham had dealt falsely with Abimelech by presenting Sarah as his sister (20:2, 9). The king has not forgotten. He has seen God’s blessing on Abraham, but he has also seen Abraham’s capacity for deception. His request is a gentle rebuke wrapped in a diplomatic proposal. There is a lesson here for God’s people: a lapse in integrity can make others wary long after it has been forgiven.

Abimelech grounds his request in what he has already done: “according to the kindness that I have done unto thee, thou shalt do unto me, and to the land wherein thou hast sojourned.” He had restored Sarah, given gifts, and invited Abraham to dwell wherever he pleased (20:14–15). Now he asks Abraham to respond in kind. The word “kindness” is ḥesed, covenant loyalty, the faithful goodness owed within a relationship. Abimelech wants their relationship placed on that footing.

The king’s mention of “the land wherein thou hast sojourned” is also significant. Abraham is still a resident alien. He owns no territory yet, though God has promised him the whole land. The treaty would give him secure footing in a region that his descendants would one day possess.

wordNotes.explanation: A rich covenant term meaning steadfast loyalty, faithful love, or kindness shown within a relationship of obligation. It describes the loyalty Rahab asks of the spies, the bond between David and Jonathan, and supremely God’s unfailing covenant love. Abimelech asks Abraham to return the loyalty he has received.

From שָׁקַר (shaqar), “to deal falsely, lie, break faith.” The related noun שֶׁקֶר (sheqer) means falsehood. The verb is used of breaking a covenant or oath. Psalm 89 uses it when God swears He will not be false to His faithfulness toward David.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham said, I will swear.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham said, I will swear.” Abraham’s answer is brief and direct. In Hebrew the pronoun “I” is expressed separately and placed first, giving the sense “I, for my part, will swear.” He commits himself without hesitation, though the next verse shows that he has a grievance to resolve before the covenant is concluded.

Abraham’s readiness to swear by God reflects his desire for peace with his neighbors. He had made alliances before, with Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner at Hebron (14:13), and he had refused gifts from the king of Sodom to keep his independence (14:23). Here, too, he enters an agreement honorably. Scripture later commends seeking peace with all people as far as possible (Romans 12:18; Hebrews 12:14). Abraham’s oath is also a step of repentance for his earlier deception: the man who once dealt falsely now pledges to deal truly.

wordNotes.term: אָנֹכִי אִשָּׁבֵעַ (ʾanokhi ʾishshaveaʿ) — I will swear
wordNotes.explanation: The verb שָׁבַע (shavaʿ) in the Niphal means to bind oneself by oath. It shares its consonants with the number seven, שֶׁבַע (shevaʿ), a connection the chapter exploits in the seven lambs and the name Beersheba. The emphatic pronoun stresses Abraham’s personal commitment.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham reproved Abimelech because of a well of water, which Abimelech's servants had violently taken away.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham reproved Abimelech because of a well of water, which Abimelech’s servants had violently taken away.” Before finalizing the treaty, Abraham raises an injustice. A well he had dug had been seized by the king’s servants. He does not swallow the wrong for the sake of a smooth agreement, nor does he retaliate. He brings the matter openly to the king who is responsible for his servants.

In the dry Negeb, wells were precious. A well meant water for flocks, servants, and family; without it a herdsman could not stay in a region. Disputes over wells were common and could escalate quickly, as Isaac would later discover when the herdsmen of Gerar contested his wells at Esek and Sitnah (26:19–21). The seizure of Abraham’s well was not a small matter. It threatened his ability to live in the land.

The verb “reproved” describes a formal complaint, the kind of argument a person brings when seeking justice. The phrase “violently taken away” uses a term for robbery or seizure by force, later used in Israel’s law for taking another’s property (Leviticus 6:2–4). Abraham’s action shows that peacemaking does not mean ignoring wrong. Lasting peace requires honesty about grievances. Jesus taught that if a brother sins against you, you should go and tell him his fault (Matthew 18:15). Abraham addresses the problem at its source.

wordNotes.explanation: From יָכַח (yakaḥ), a verb used in legal settings for arguing a case, correcting, or rebuking. It can mean to decide between parties or to set right. Leviticus uses it in the command to rebuke a neighbor rather than harbor hatred. Abraham lodges a formal complaint to obtain justice.

From גָּזַל (gazal), “to seize, rob, take by force.” It describes the forcible seizure of what belongs to someone else. Israel’s law forbids it and requires restitution. The word makes clear that Abraham’s complaint concerns a real wrong, not a misunderstanding.

verses.bibleText: And Abimelech said, I wot not who hath done this thing: neither didst thou tell me, neither yet heard I of it, but to day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abimelech said, I wot not who hath done this thing: neither didst thou tell me, neither yet heard I of it, but to day.” Abimelech answers with a triple denial: he does not know who did it, Abraham never told him, and he had heard nothing until now. The response sounds sincere, but it also shifts some responsibility back onto Abraham for not raising the matter sooner.

Whether Abimelech was truly ignorant is impossible to know. A ruler might well be unaware of a quarrel among shepherds far from his town. Still, his protest echoes his earlier defense before God, when he insisted on the integrity of his heart (20:5). The narrative leaves the question open and focuses instead on the resolution. Abimelech does not deny the wrong, and he does not refuse to set it right. His answer opens the way for the covenant to address the problem directly.

The exchange is a reminder that misunderstandings and hidden grievances can undermine relationships. Abimelech’s words, “neither didst thou tell me,” suggest that the matter might have been resolved earlier if Abraham had spoken. Honest communication guards peace.

wordNotes.term: לֹא יָדַעְתִּי (loʾ yadaʿti) — I wot not
wordNotes.explanation: “I did not know.” The verb יָדַע (yadaʿ) covers knowledge gained by experience and awareness. Abimelech’s claim of ignorance places the blame on his servants and opens the way for a settlement without loss of royal honor.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham took sheep and oxen, and gave them unto Abimelech; and both of them made a covenant.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham took sheep and oxen, and gave them unto Abimelech; and both of them made a covenant.” Abraham now takes the initiative. In chapter 20 Abimelech had given Abraham sheep, oxen, and servants (20:14); now Abraham gives sheep and oxen to Abimelech. The roles have reversed. The sojourner who once received gifts as compensation now gives as an equal, or even as the stronger party.

The animals may have served as a gift sealing the friendship, or they may have been used in the ceremony of covenant-making itself. The Hebrew expression “made a covenant” literally means “cut a covenant,” recalling the ritual of chapter 15, where animals were divided and the parties passed between the pieces (15:9–18; Jeremiah 34:18–19). Such rites signified that those who broke the agreement would deserve the fate of the slain animals. Whatever the precise ceremony, the covenant was formal and binding.

This is the first recorded treaty between Abraham and a foreign king. It secured peace and allowed Abraham to dwell safely in the region. Yet it was a human covenant, and it would not last forever. In Isaac’s time the Philistines would stop up Abraham’s wells (26:15), and a new treaty would be needed (26:28–31). Human covenants depend on human faithfulness. God’s covenant with Abraham rested on God’s own oath and could not fail (Hebrews 6:13–18).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּכְרְתוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם בְּרִית (wayyikretu shenehem berit) — and both of them made a covenant
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “and the two of them cut a covenant.” The verb כָּרַת (karat), “to cut,” is the standard expression for making a covenant, probably from the ritual of cutting sacrificial animals. בְּרִית (berit) denotes a binding agreement with obligations, whether between equals, between a king and vassal, or between God and His people.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock by themselves.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock by themselves.” After the general exchange of animals, Abraham does something unexpected. He separates seven female lambs and sets them apart. The action is deliberately visible, designed to provoke a question.

Ewe lambs were valuable, since they represented the future growth of a flock, so the gesture was costly as well as symbolic. The number also carries meaning. In Hebrew “seven” (shevaʿ) and “swear” (shavaʿ) share the same consonants, and the chapter plays on the connection. The seven lambs will serve a purpose distinct from the covenant animals of verse 27: they will stand as a public witness to Abraham’s claim to the well. Seven often signified completeness, so the number may also express the fullness and finality of the agreement. Abraham is not content with a general promise of goodwill. He wants the specific wrong of verse 25 settled in a way no one can later dispute.

wordNotes.term: שֶׁבַע כִּבְשֹׂת (shevaʿ kivsot) — seven ewe lambs
wordNotes.explanation: כִּבְשָׂה (kivsah) is a female lamb, the same word used in Nathan’s parable of the poor man’s one little ewe lamb. The number שֶׁבַע (shevaʿ), “seven,” echoes the verb “swear” and prepares for the name Beersheba.

verses.bibleText: And Abimelech said unto Abraham, What mean these seven ewe lambs which thou hast set by themselves?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abimelech said unto Abraham, What mean these seven ewe lambs which thou hast set by themselves?” Abimelech responds exactly as Abraham intended. He notices the separated lambs and asks their meaning. The question gives Abraham the opportunity to state his claim formally in front of the king and his commander.

The form of the question resembles later moments in Israel’s history when visible signs were meant to prompt inquiry. The memorial stones at the Jordan were set up so that children would ask, “What mean ye by these stones?” (Joshua 4:6), and the Passover ritual invited the question, “What mean ye by this service?” (Exodus 12:26). A visible act, followed by a question and an answer, fixes an event in public memory. Abraham uses the same method to make his right to the well a matter of record.

wordNotes.term: מָה הֵנָּה (mah hennah) — what mean these
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “what are these?” The simple question asks for the significance of what is seen. Similar questions in Exodus, Deuteronomy, and Joshua introduce explanations of signs and memorials that preserve the meaning of God’s acts for later generations.

verses.bibleText: And he said, For these seven ewe lambs shalt thou take of my hand, that they may be a witness unto me, that I have digged this well.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he said, For these seven ewe lambs shalt thou take of my hand, that they may be a witness unto me, that I have digged this well.” Abraham explains the purpose of the lambs. By accepting them, Abimelech publicly acknowledges that Abraham dug the well and has the right to it. The lambs are not a purchase price in the ordinary sense, but a legal token. Once the king receives them, he cannot later deny Abraham’s claim, and neither can his servants.

The phrase “a witness unto me” shows how covenants were confirmed in the ancient world. Physical objects served as evidence of an agreement: a heap of stones between Jacob and Laban (31:44–52), a great stone under an oak at Shechem (Joshua 24:26–27), an altar named “Ed,” witness, by the eastern tribes (Joshua 22:34). Abraham’s living witnesses would graze in Abimelech’s flocks, a constant reminder of what had been agreed.

The words “I have digged this well” are emphatic. Abraham’s labor gave him the right to the water. In a land he did not yet possess, the well was a small piece of the promise secured. It anticipated the day when his descendants would inherit the whole land, and Isaac would later reopen the wells his father had dug and call them by the names Abraham had given them (26:18). A well in the desert, secured by honest dealing and public witness, became a sign that God’s promises were taking root in the soil of Canaan.

wordNotes.explanation: עֵדָה (ʿedah) is a feminine form related to עֵד (ʿed), “witness.” It denotes a testimony or piece of evidence that confirms an agreement. The heap of stones between Jacob and Laban and the stone at Shechem function the same way, giving lasting testimony to a sworn covenant.

From חָפַר (ḥafar), “to dig.” Digging a well required great labor in hard ground and established a claim to the water. The same verb recurs in chapter 26, where Isaac’s servants dig and redig wells and contend over them with the herdsmen of Gerar.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore he called that place Beer-sheba; because there they sware both of them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Wherefore he called that place Beer-sheba; because there they sware both of them.” The name gathers up the whole transaction. Beersheba means “well of seven” or “well of the oath,” and both meanings fit. Seven lambs were given, and an oath was sworn. The Hebrew sound play makes the place itself a monument to the agreement. Anyone who spoke the name would recall that Abraham’s right to the water had been confirmed by sworn covenant.

Beersheba became one of the most important places in Israel’s history. It marked the southern extent of the land, and the expression “from Dan even to Beer-sheba” described the whole country from north to south (Judges 20:1; 1 Samuel 3:20). Isaac would later live there, and God would appear to him there with the promise, “Fear not, for I am with thee” (26:23–25). Jacob would offer sacrifices there before going down to Egypt, and God would speak to him in a night vision (46:1–4). The well that Abraham dug became a center of the patriarchs’ life and worship.

In Genesis 26:33 Isaac names a well Shebah, and the narrator says “therefore the name of the city is Beer-sheba unto this day.” That later naming reaffirms the earlier one after the wells had been stopped and reopened. The repeated association of oath and well shows how God’s faithfulness was remembered through ordinary places.

The name also points to a deeper truth. God Himself swore to Abraham by His own name (22:16), and Hebrews explains that by “two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie,” His promise and His oath, believers have strong consolation (Hebrews 6:17–18). Abraham’s oath with Abimelech secured a well; God’s oath to Abraham secured the hope of the world.

wordNotes.explanation: בְּאֵר (beʾer) means a well or pit dug to reach water. שֶׁבַע (shevaʿ) is the number seven, and the verb שָׁבַע (shavaʿ) means to swear. The name can thus be heard as “well of seven” or “well of the oath.” The narrator connects it explicitly with the oath (“because there they sware”), while the seven lambs supply the numerical echo.

The Niphal of שָׁבַע (shavaʿ), meaning to bind oneself by oath. The plural, “both of them,” confirms that the commitment was mutual. Hebrews notes that people swear by something greater than themselves, and that an oath ends all dispute.

verses.bibleText: Thus they made a covenant at Beer-sheba: then Abimelech rose up, and Phichol the chief captain of his host, and they returned into the land of the Philistines.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Thus they made a covenant at Beer-sheba: then Abimelech rose up, and Phichol the chief captain of his host, and they returned into the land of the Philistines.” The verse summarizes and closes the negotiation. The covenant has been made, the oath sworn, and the visitors return home. Peace has been established.

The statement that Abimelech returned “into the land of the Philistines” suggests that Beersheba lay at the edge of or beyond his core territory, though within his sphere of influence. The Philistines best known from the time of the judges arrived later in force, but people from the Aegean and Mediterranean world were already settling along the southern coast of Canaan in the patriarchal era. Genesis applies to them the name by which the region was later known. Abimelech’s Gerar was a smaller, more peaceable community than the warlike Philistine cities of Samson’s and David’s day.

The treaty with Abimelech illustrates how Abraham lived as a stranger among the nations. He did not seize land or fight his neighbors. He dug wells, made honest agreements, and trusted God for the future. Jesus called peacemakers blessed (Matthew 5:9), and Abraham’s conduct at Beersheba shows what that can look like for a pilgrim whose hope rests on God’s promise rather than on human power.

wordNotes.term: אֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים (ʾerets pelishtim) — the land of the Philistines
wordNotes.explanation: This is the first time the phrase appears in Scripture. The Philistines are traced in the Table of Nations to the Casluhim and associated with Caphtor, probably Crete. The name designates people of Aegean origin settled along the southern coast of Canaan, of whom Abimelech’s Gerar represents an early community.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham planted a grove in Beer-sheba, and called there on the name of the LORD, the everlasting God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham planted a grove in Beer-sheba.” The KJV word “grove” can mislead readers, since elsewhere it translates a different Hebrew word for the sacred poles of Canaanite worship (Deuteronomy 16:21). The word here is ʾeshel, a tamarisk tree. Tamarisks are hardy, deep-rooted trees suited to the dry Negeb; they grow slowly, live long, and provide shade. Abraham planted one at Beersheba, probably as a memorial of the covenant and a sign of his intention to remain in the region. Planting a slow-growing tree is an act of faith in the future. Saul later held court under a tamarisk at Gibeah, and his bones were buried beneath one at Jabesh (1 Samuel 22:6; 31:13).

“And called there on the name of the LORD.” Wherever Abraham settled, he worshiped. At Shechem, Bethel, and Hebron he built altars and called on the LORD’s name (12:7–8; 13:4, 18). The expression describes public worship and proclamation, acknowledging God openly before the household and neighbors. Beersheba becomes not only a place of treaty but a place of worship. The peace secured by the covenant allows Abraham to honor God freely in the land.

He calls on God as “the everlasting God.” This is the only time this title appears in Genesis. Earlier Abraham knew God as “the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth” (14:22) and as “God Almighty” (17:1). Here he worships the God who endures through all ages. The title fits the moment. Abraham has just made a covenant with a king whose descendants would forget it within a generation. The tamarisk he planted would one day die. His own life was moving toward its close. But the God he worshiped is without beginning or end, and His promises outlast every human treaty.

Isaiah takes up the same title to comfort a weary people: “Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?” (Isaiah 40:28). Moses sings of the God who is “from everlasting to everlasting” (Psalm 90:2). Paul closes Romans by praising “the everlasting God” who has made the gospel known to all nations (Romans 16:26). The God whom Abraham worshiped under a tamarisk in the desert is the same God who fulfilled His promise through Christ and who will one day bring His people into the everlasting kingdom.

wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes the tamarisk, a tree of dry regions with small scale-like leaves and deep roots. It appears only here and in the accounts of Saul. The KJV rendering “grove” probably reflects the old understanding of the word, but the Hebrew points to a single tree, a living memorial rather than a sacred grove of the kind later forbidden in Israel.

wordNotes.term: אֵל עוֹלָם (ʾel ʿolam) — the everlasting God
wordNotes.explanation: עוֹלָם (ʿolam) refers to time extending beyond view, often translated “for ever” or “everlasting.” Joined with אֵל (ʾel), God, it describes the God whose existence and faithfulness have no limit in time. The title complements other names Abraham uses, such as El Elyon and El Shaddai, each fitting a particular revelation of God’s character. The Greek Old Testament renders it theos aiōnios, the phrase Paul uses in Romans 16:26.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham sojourned in the Philistines' land many days.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham sojourned in the Philistines’ land many days.” The chapter closes with a quiet summary. After the birth of Isaac, the departure of Ishmael, and the covenant with Abimelech, Abraham settles into a long period of peace. He stays “many days,” enough time for Isaac to grow from a weaned child into a young man by the events of chapter 22.

Yet the verb is “sojourned,” not “settled” or “possessed.” Abraham remains a resident alien, living by permission in a land God had promised to him and his descendants. He has a well, a tree, an altar, and a treaty, but not the land itself. Hebrews describes this pilgrim life: “By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise: for he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Hebrews 11:9–10).

The verse reminds believers that they, too, are strangers and pilgrims on earth (1 Peter 2:11). Like Abraham, they live in peace with neighbors where possible, worship the everlasting God openly, and wait in faith for the inheritance God has promised: not a strip of land in the Negeb, but a new earth where God will dwell with His people. The “many days” of Abraham’s sojourn were days of quiet faithfulness, and they prepared him for the greatest test of his life.

wordNotes.explanation: From גּוּר (gur), “to dwell as a resident alien.” The verb describes someone living in a place without the rights of a native. It frames Abraham’s years in the Philistines’ land, as it framed his arrival in Gerar in 20:1, reminding the reader that even in peace and prosperity he remained a pilgrim awaiting God’s promise.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What does it do to a person’s faith to wait twenty-five years for a promise, and how does the fulfilment change the way that person laughs?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God fulfils His word precisely and in His own time; the heir of promise must be received by faith and protected from what mocks it, while God’s mercy still follows those who stand outside the chosen line.
discussionQuestions: How does the threefold stress on God’s word in verses 1–2 shape the way we read the birth of Isaac?
What is the difference between Sarah’s laughter in 18:12 and her laughter in 21:6, and what produced the change?
Why does God tell Abraham to heed Sarah here when listening to her in chapter 16 led to grief?
What does God’s care for Hagar and Ishmael teach about His character toward people outside the covenant line?
How does Abraham’s treaty with Abimelech model honesty, peacemaking, and worship in a world that does not share our faith?
commonMisunderstandings: Ishmael was not a small child carried on Hagar’s shoulder; the chronology makes him a youth of about sixteen or seventeen, and the provisions were what Abraham placed on her shoulder.
God’s approval of Sarah’s demand does not bless every attitude behind it; it confirms that the inheritance belongs to Isaac by promise.
The sending away of Ishmael is not God’s rejection of him as a person; God hears him, promises him a nation, and remains with him.
The “grove” of verse 33 was not a pagan sacred grove; Abraham planted a tamarisk as a lasting memorial where he worshiped the true God.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep God’s faithfulness at the center: Isaac is born because God spoke, the household is ordered by God’s word, the outcast lives because God hears, and the land is entered in peace because God is with Abraham.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Receive the promised Son by faith as Abraham received Isaac, turn from the laughter of doubt and scorn to the laughter of grace, and trust the Everlasting God who hears you even in the wilderness.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Salvation comes by God’s promise and power, fulfilled in Christ the true Seed, and is received by faith rather than produced by human effort.
flow: God made a promise that only He could keep, and He kept it at the exact time He had set.
Isaac, born by divine power to parents past hope, pictures the birth of Christ, who came “when the fulness of the time was come.”
The son born by human planning cannot share the inheritance with the son of promise; salvation cannot be part grace and part self-effort.
Yet God still hears the cry of the outcast and opens eyes to the water of life close at hand.
Every person is invited to become a child of promise by faith in Christ and to worship the Everlasting God.
simpleIllustrations: A letter postmarked years ago that arrives on the very morning it was dated for shows that the sender planned the timing; Isaac’s birth arrived on God’s appointed day after decades of waiting.
A traveler dying of thirst beside a covered well does not need new water but opened eyes; Hagar’s rescue pictures how God shows us the grace that was near all along.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you stop trying to secure God’s blessing by your own plans and receive it as a gift through Jesus Christ, the promised Seed?
cautions: Do not present Hagar and Ishmael merely as villains; the text shows God’s compassion toward them.
Do not turn Paul’s use of the story in Galatians into hostility toward any people; his point concerns two ways of seeking God’s favor.
Avoid implying that God’s timing always means long delay; the lesson is that His timing is wise and certain.

reflectionQuestions: Which of God’s promises am I tempted to laugh at because the waiting has been long?
Where have I tried to manufacture by my own plans what God said He would give?
Is there anything in my life that mocks God’s work and needs to be sent away?
When I feel abandoned in a wilderness, do I remember that God hears me “where I am”?
How can I pursue honest peace with neighbors who do not share my faith while still calling on the name of the LORD?
